input: The lifetime values that have been reported for the benchmark material divide along the conditions under which they were measured, and much of the apparent disagreement between them narrows once those conditions are set side by side. One group reports lifetimes from tests that were held at steady state: fresh samples, a constant feed, and an end of life set by the first measurable loss of capacity. The other group, by contrast, cycled its samples between loading and regeneration and took the lifetime at a fixed loss of working capacity, so its figures accumulate the damage of repeated cycling that the steady tests never impose. Part of the gap between the two sets of values is therefore definitional in nature. A lifetime counted to first loss and a lifetime counted to a fixed loss are different quantities, and the same material cannot really be expected to return the same number under both definitions. The cycled figures also carry a further difference: capacity loss under cycling includes losses at the binder and at particle contacts, which a steady test on a fresh sample does not reach, so the cycled values come out lower for reasons that sit partly outside the sorbent itself. Weighed on the test conditions, the preference here is for the cycled values as the design basis, and that preference rests on one condition: that the duty in service cycles the benchmark material in the same way, with regeneration as a routine step rather than an occasional recovery. Where the duty is a single pass to breakthrough with no regeneration, the steady-state values are the closer match and the preference reverses. Neither set of values speaks to behaviour once mechanical attrition in a moving bed becomes the limiting mechanism, and on that point the published record offers nothing to weigh, because
